# Targeted accessibility actions (Core prerequisite)

Portable Core now queues `CUI_ACCESSIBILITY_FOCUS` and
`CUI_ACCESSIBILITY_ACTIVATE` by stable `cui_id`, without pointer coordinates or
synthetic keyboard input. This is an action-routing prerequisite; it does not
register a native accessibility tree or provide an OS/screen-reader bridge.

```c
if (cui_accessibility_action_supported(ui, button_id, CUI_ACCESSIBILITY_ACTIVATE)) {
    bool admitted = cui_queue_accessibility_action(ui, button_id, CUI_ACCESSIBILITY_ACTIVATE);
    /* Check admitted and cui_last_error(ui); admission is not execution. */
}
```

Call both APIs between frames on the context's owning thread. The query reads
only the last completed semantic snapshot and returns false during an open frame.
Queueing during a frame reports `CUI_ERROR_LIFECYCLE`. Invalid action enums, zero,
missing, disabled, modal-blocked or unsupported targets report appended
`CUI_ERROR_INVALID_ACTION`. The shared input queue holds 256 events; a valid action
when full reports `CUI_ERROR_CAPACITY`. Failure appends nothing and changes no
focus, activation, pointer or capture state. Errors follow the existing sticky
Core error contract; `cui_clear_error` permits callers to acknowledge rejected
external requests without poisoning later work. No platform/Clay types or
borrowed payload are needed. Existing enum ordinals and zero event initializers
remain intact.

The new event type is `CUI_EVENT_ACCESSIBILITY_ACTION`; its appended
`accessibility_target` and `accessibility_action` fields provide distinct source
provenance. Direct `cui_queue_event` submission of that event uses identical
validation, and unrelated pointer/key/text fields are discarded. No OS callback
may call these APIs concurrently; a future native adapter must copy requests and
drain them on the main thread.

## Supported targets and delivery

Focus uses Core's normal focusability rules, including explicit `focusable`
containers and programmatic-only (`tab_index == -1`) controls. `no_focus` and
disabled IDs are rejected. It makes focus visible, preserving pointer and Space
captures, and respects the published modal scope. Passive label focus proxies
are not silently redirected; submit their actual eligible target ID.

Default Activate roles are Button, Link, Checkbox, Switch, Radio, MenuItem,
MenuItemCheckbox and MenuItemRadio. An explicit `pointer_activatable` semantic
also opts in, including `no_focus` pointer-only controls. Activate does not move
focus, pointer position or capture. Textbox, Slider, Scrollbar, Tab, Option,
TreeItem, table headers/grid cells and passive containers have no default
Activate capability in this first increment. Focus remains available where
eligible. Consumers that opt into a custom activation capability must implement
that action rather than rely on keyboard-only handlers.

Dispatch revalidates the completed target and produces normal
`cui_event_target`/`cui_event_activation` metadata and pending activation slots.
Widget submission checks current disabled state, semantic role and active modal
scope. Current inert/layout-only or removed targets cannot retain a pending
action into another frame; completion withdraws their metadata. A removed or
newly disabled Focus target restores the prior surviving focus where possible,
without overriding a subsequent explicit focus change. Removal of multiple queued
Focus targets unwinds in reverse order. Accepted queue admission therefore does
not guarantee the widget will still be eligible or submitted in that frame.

Stable IDs represent stable logical widgets: use a new ID for a new widget
identity. Core cannot distinguish replacement with an identical ID/role and no
intervening completed removal. Capability details are declared in semantic
submission after `cui_interact`; admission follows their published snapshot.
Current disabled/role/scope checks are immediate, while final semantic withdrawal
occurs at frame completion. Applications should keep published action capability
consistent with their current reducer and must not perform speculative external
side effects during layout-only passes.

## Consumption and existing activation semantics

Simple controls consume pending activation through their normal `cui_interact`
path; actual styled button and checkbox tests verify callback/value changes.
No request is replayed on an idle frame. Multiple same-ID pending activations
coalesce into one `activated` boolean in a frame, exactly as existing pointer/key
activations do. Individual event-aware reducers can inspect each event. Queue
requests across frames if separate callbacks are required from a boolean API.

A deferred/capture-phase owner may handle the event and call `cui_consume_event`.
For the new accessibility event, consumption also cancels its pending activation
and clears activation metadata, so a subsequently submitted widget cannot replay
that callback. Ordinary input consumption behavior is unchanged.
`cui_cancel_event_activation` suppresses activation alone while retaining the
event target, matching its existing capture-phase contract. Deferred handlers
must check consumption and validated activation, not event type alone.

## Compound reducer audit and verification

Read-only source audit found Tabs and List selection reducers keep an event-local
cursor and reset it to the explicit target only for pointer-up. Multiple targeted
accessibility activations can select an earlier cursor; these roles are therefore
Focus-only by default pending assigned base fixes. Menu reducers generally use
activation metadata but have not received native accessibility acceptance here.
Tree/table reducers also inspect activation metadata; full selection, expansion,
scroll and value/text actions need independent family tests. No base/component
implementation was changed, and no full compound-family support is claimed.

Headless Core tests exercise actual styled button/checkbox scenes, separate target
and focus, same-ID coalescing, consumed/deferred/cancelled activations, invalid
enums, queue capacity, programmatic-only stops, Tab and pointer-only eligibility,
removed/reintroduced/changed-role targets, current-frame disabled/modal/inert
rejection, ordered Focus plus keyboard events, focus rollback, and preserved
pointer/Space capture. Full warning build and CTest run: 90/91 pass; only expected
stale generated distribution fails. Four focused sanitizer checks (Core, base,
components, choice) pass. Native transport/screen-reader validation
belongs to the optional bridge implementation, not this prerequisite.

# Build CUI applications with an AI agent

Give an agent your application requirements and the repository's current API and tests. CUI is a portable C11 library with optional host/renderer adapters. The live gallery covers 78 entries, while the feature manifest still records incomplete reference behavior.

## Install the CUI skill

```sh
npx skills add mattmezza/cui --skill cui
```

The repository distributes `skills/cui/SKILL.md` with Python 3.9+ standard-library
helpers and generated offline references. Ask your agent to use the CUI skill to
build your app. It covers native C11, browser/WASM, embedding and language
builders, including backend selection, fonts, responsive layout and limitations.
The skill checks prerequisites without installing packages. Setup pins a source
commit; subsequent discovery must use that project's `--source` path to avoid
mixing API revisions. See the skill for search, API lookup, vendoring, existing
example setup and integrity-check commands. Python helpers need no pip packages.

Maintainers regenerate resources with `python scripts/generate_agent_skill.py`;
CI checks freshness and exercises an installed copy outside the repository.

## Consumer setup prompt

```text
Build my UI using the CUI repository at https://github.com/mattmezza/cui.
My application requirements: [describe the screens, interactions and host].

Start by reading README.md, docs/START_HERE.md,
docs/IMMEDIATE_AND_STATE.md, docs/INTERFACES.md and docs/gpui-parity.json.
For adaptive layouts read docs/RESPONSIVE_LAYOUT.md and docs/LAYOUT_GUIDE.md.
For reusable text styles read docs/TYPOGRAPHY_TOKENS.md and docs/TYPOGRAPHY.md.
Use the current public headers as the API authority; do not invent symbols.
Check the feature status and limitations for every component you choose.

Use portable C11 for CUI integration. Keep platform and renderer code in host
adapters. Keep application values, buffers and explicit component models alive
across frames. Use stable IDs and balance every successful begin/end pair.
Render borrowed draw data before starting the next frame. Connect actions using
return-value events or the documented controlled callbacks.

For the native source bundle, read README.md and vendor/include/cui/cui.h.
Edit app.c for portable UI; main.c owns the native host. Run make with warnings.
Use APP_SOURCES for additional C files and TARGET for the executable name.
For Linux automation use an invisible Xvfb display; never DISPLAY=:0 or the
maintainer's Wayland session. Browser automation must be headless.

For browser work build the real WASM gallery and exercise actual interactions. Report what ran, what remains incomplete, and
which renderer/platform was tested. Do not claim full parity or platform support
from an API declaration, compilation or a screenshot alone.
```

Replace the application-requirements line before sending the prompt. The source repository's AGENTS.md and your current task instructions determine the engineering workflow.

## Repository maintainer workflow

Consumers need the bundle's compiler/Make/system-library prerequisites, not the
repository toolchain. Maintainers additionally read `AGENTS.md`, use isolated
worktrees for workers with explicit file ownership, and let only the integrator
merge. Preserve unrelated changes and all 78 manifest entries. Add meaningful
headless tests for behavior changes and compile with warnings:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja
cmake --build build
python scripts/test_local.py --build-dir build
```

The wrapper runs CTest under invisible Xvfb on Linux; never fall back to the
maintainer's desktop. GPU hardware checks unsupported there remain deferred.
For distribution changes run `python scripts/amalgamate.py` and the repository's
lint, format and distribution checks. Use current public headers as API authority,
then [Layout](LAYOUT_GUIDE.md), [IDs/lifetimes](IDS_AND_LIFETIMES.md) and
[Debugging](DEBUGGING.md). Respect Core → base → components; adapters depend on
Core. Do not introduce platform/Clay types into public APIs.

## Download documentation without browser rendering

The built website publishes:

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `llms.txt` | A concise overview and Markdown links to documentation |
| `llms-full.txt` | The documentation bundle with source attribution and current catalog data |
| `llm.txt` / `llm-full.txt` | Aliases using the filenames requested for this website |
| `markdown/…` | Plain Markdown documents generated from the same repository content |
| `catalog.json` | All 78 entries, feature statuses and limitations |
| `headers/<basename>.h` | Exact byte copies of this build's public headers; API authority |
| `api-index.json` | Public symbol names and declarations with links to exported headers |
| `build-info.json` | Source revision, build profile and header/document SHA-256 hashes |
| `tasks/native-app.md`, `tasks/layout.md`, `tasks/debugging.md` | Focused guide bundles for common tasks |
| `docs-index.md` | Full document index, including historical material |
| `docs.json` | Document Markdown links, descriptions, keywords and historical flags |

Start with `llms.txt` or a focused task bundle, then fetch the exact public header
for a declaration. `api-index.json` supplies a `source_revision` and a `symbols`
array with `name`, `declaration` and relative `header` links. `build-info.json`
records `source_revision`, `build_profile`, `headers_sha256`,
`documentation_sha256` and `api_authority`; use these to identify the exported
revision rather than mixing headers from another release. Source links are pinned
to that revision.

Use the full bundle when your tool can accommodate it. `llms-full.txt` excludes
documents marked historical, including development/validation reports. They
remain available through `docs-index.md` and their `markdown/docs/*.md` exports;
`docs.json` carries the `historical` flag. Historical reports are evidence for
their recorded checkpoint, not current API or platform guarantees. The current
headers and feature manifest take precedence.

The index follows the [llms.txt proposal](https://llmstxt.org/). Publishing these files supplies readable documentation; it does not establish a search-ranking result or guarantee that an agent understands every API.

## Ask for evidence

For a UI change, request the triggering interaction, expected result, meaningful test and actual running screenshot. For a host integration, request a buildable example, its memory/lifetime contract and the observed backend. For another language, distinguish a tested FFI or WASM example from a proposed binding.

## Keep API documentation synchronized

When changing a public API, update both the human guide and agent-facing
references in the same change. Add or refresh a guide when composition requires
more than a signature, update examples and meaningful tests, and verify the
website exports the exact public header plus its `api-index.json` declaration.
Header-only inline APIs belong in that index too. The generated `llms.txt`,
`llms-full.txt` and focused task bundles must expose the relevant guide; do not
edit generated website files instead of the repository sources.

For responsive UI, query current container widths in logical units and preserve
one application state across breakpoint changes. Omit hidden control subtrees or
use the documented input/semantic suppression contracts. For typography, resolve
caller-owned roles and register actual faces on the shared measurement/render
font owner. Report unsupported tracking, variable-axis or gradient-paint requests
as roadmap work rather than inventing token fields.

The responsive dashboard's native launcher depends on the SDL3 callback runner.
Consult `cui_sdl3.h` and the native starter guide for the shipped runner/manual
pump and live-resize contract. A passing portable layout test validates neither a
native event loop nor a browser rendering backend.

For SDL3 applications, prefer `cui_sdl3_run` for callback-driven composition during
OS-managed modal resize. Manual `cui_sdl3_poll` loops remain supported, but their
next frame can wait until the operating system releases its modal event pump.
Inside runner callbacks, `cui_sdl3_poll` synchronizes IME/cursor state without
recursively pumping events. See [Live resize](LIVE_RESIZE.md) for lifecycle,
threading, frame scheduling and scoped native validation details.

# Alert and Bubble slots

Source audit: GPUI Kit 0.7.1, commit `87d10ae5e1299d1be18670a37570c5402f952e34`, `crates/component/src/alert.rs` and `bubble.rs`. This is an original C implementation inspired by those contracts.

Alert retains INFO as its zero kind. `CUI_ALERT_DEFAULT` adds a neutral surface. Info, success, warning and error use the corresponding theme foreground, border and tinted surface. A banner removes the border/radius and omits title text and the title callback. `title_content`, `content`, and `action` replace or extend the text slots in that order. Dismissal still returns activation and optionally changes caller-owned `visible`.

`cui_bubble()` accepts message text or a custom `content` callback, incoming/outgoing alignment, an optional reaction callback and top/bottom ordering. Filled text uses `on_primary`; semantic variants use their kind foreground. Secondary/muted use a subdued neutral surface; outline uses background and border; ghost removes surface and padding. `cui_bubble_foreground()` supplies the same foreground when composing through the legacy begin/end API.

```c
cui_bubble(ui, id, theme, (cui_bubble_options){
    .variant = CUI_BUBBLE_SUCCESS,
    .alignment = CUI_BUBBLE_OUTGOING,
    .width = 400,
    .message = cui_string("Saved successfully"),
    .announcement = CUI_BUBBLE_ANNOUNCE_POLITE
});
```

Callbacks run synchronously with borrowed context/theme and a semantic foreground. Use percentage-width boxes to fit the current parent; a callback must balance all begin/end calls and must provide its own controls through base-backed components. Custom text chooses the supplied foreground explicitly. Supply `accessible_name` when custom content has no message text. Callback/user storage remains caller-owned; no retained allocation occurs. Invalid Bubble enums omit the component.

The convenience Bubble reserves up to 80% of its row for the surface (100% for ghost) and aligns its content within that region. A positive width specifies row width; zero uses parent width. With `state == NULL`, reactions occupy normal flow above/below, aligned along the row. Supply a unique zero-initialized caller-owned `cui_bubble_state` to measure the first frame and settle an overlapping pill on the selected surface edge. The pill extends three quarters of its height outside the surface, reserves room within the row to keep adjacent bubbles from covering controls, and inherits ancestor clipping. Geometry changes request a bounded measurement redraw; changes to custom slot content require incrementing `content_revision`. Width, variant, alignment, reaction presence and theme font/padding changes trigger measurement automatically. The cache must not be shared between IDs. Exact first-frame anchored placement is not promised: Core has no current-frame measured-anchor attachment primitive. There is no separate BubbleGroup API; compose a column using existing layout boxes. These remain explicit parity gaps.

Alert publishes ALERT; Bubble defaults to a passive GROUP, with POLITE mapping to STATUS and ASSERTIVE to ALERT. These roles request semantics only. Actual announcements depend on host/native/browser accessibility adapters and are not proven by headless role tests. No reaction area itself becomes a tab stop; controls composed within it preserve their own button semantics.

Headless evidence: `tests/unit/test_alert_bubble_slots.c` exercises both themes, every Alert kind/Bubble variant, slot ordering, incoming/outgoing placement, top/bottom reactions, first-frame measurement and settled overlap without perpetual redraw, passive status semantics and disabled action controls. Existing content tests cover controlled dismissal. The gallery Bubble story demonstrates semantic kinds, alignment and measured reaction pills. `tests/web/test_alert_bubble_slots.py` checks actual WASM paint colors, placement and reaction ordering at desktop/mobile widths. Pointer/Enter activation is covered headlessly and real Chromium CDP touch toggles are covered in the browser. Native screen-reader announcement delivery remains unverified.

# Alert completed-dismiss observations

Include `cui/cui_alert_events.h` and call `cui_alert_events` to observe the
built-in Dismiss action. This additive native C facade calls the existing
`cui_alert` once. Its original options, Button style, content/action slots,
visibility assignment, drawing and bool result remain unchanged.

```c
static void dismissed(void *user, const cui_alert_dismissal *event) {
    app_state *state = user;
    state->last_dismissal = *event; /* Pointer-free copy. */
    state->dismissals++;
}

cui_alert_dismiss_result result = cui_alert_events(
    ui, alert_id, &theme,
    (cui_alert_options){.kind = CUI_ALERT_INFO,
                        .message = cui_string("Saved"),
                        .visible = &state.visible, .dismissible = true},
    (cui_alert_dismiss_handler){dismissed, &state});
```

The [standalone headless example](../examples/alert_events/main.c) shows the
complete setup. Link the usual `cui` library; no new dispatch service or retained
listener registration is required.

`legacy_dismissed` is exactly the old aggregate bool. `dismissal_count` is zero
or one for an eligible completed built-in dismissal, including when no callback
is installed. A callback runs at most once per invocation, even when multiple
accepted inputs activate Dismiss. Choose the callback or result for each side
effect; reading the result never invokes or replays a callback.

Observation occurs synchronously after the old function has ended its Alert box
and, if supplied, assigned `*visible=false`. `visibility_assigned` records that
assignment, even if a render slot already set the value false. It does not claim
a transition or closed lifecycle. Without visibility storage, accepted dismissal
still returns true and can notify; `visibility_assigned` is false. The owner
still decides whether to omit the Alert next frame.

Visibility is checked once at entry. Title/body/action slots retain their old
order and may change owner visibility or consume input before the Dismiss Button.
A slot changing visibility alone does not synthesize a completion. Consuming an
input uses existing Core policy: it cancels the tested accessibility action but
does not revoke an ordinary already-accepted Enter-down activation. The facade
adds no general input-cancellation promise. The observer
can set visibility true again; no second assignment or veto follows, and the
frozen completion result stays unchanged. Slot `options.user` and handler `user`
are independent. Invalid arguments produce `valid=false`; initially hidden
Alerts are valid omissions with `submitted=false`. Passive inert/layout-only
submission preserves legacy behavior but has no eligible observation/count.

The payload's common metadata has `kind=ACTIVATE`, public Alert ID, actual entry
frame, `UNKNOWN` source, and only `HAS_FRAME`. There is no per-input event index,
activation snapshot, pointer/touch coordinate, source, close reason or timestamp.
Even a single accepted input does not upgrade this aggregate metadata. Actual
input routing stays in the existing Button. Custom action-slot child events are
separate and are not Alert dismissals.

Options, handler and active eligibility/frame are copied at entry. Payload views
are borrowed synchronously; a copied payload outlives the frame/context. Keep
visibility, UI/theme, slot resources and users alive through their existing
submission/rendering lifetimes. Do not recurse into UI submission, destroy the
context, free/rebind active resources or unwind through C callbacks. Request
teardown in application state and perform it after the frame.

This native slice does not provide per-input callbacks, controlled dismissal,
veto/default cancellation, retained open/close policy, AlertDialog forwarding,
async listeners or a Python/Node/TypeScript/Go/Rust observer binding. The retained
bridge's existing Alert does not configure native dismissibility/visibility;
its foreign queued notifications do not implement this observer contract.
See the [design checkpoint](design/ALERT_EVENTS_SLICE.md) and
[binding coverage](design/COMPONENT_EVENTS_BINDINGS.md).

The focused headless regression covers pointer/touch, Enter/Space, genuine Core
accessibility activation, multiple accepted inputs, callback-independent counts,
no visibility storage, slot/observer owner writes, omission/passive submission,
custom actions, copied payload lifetime, legacy shape/SVG software pixels,
text command geometry/style/content and semantics. Font rasterization is not
exercised by the portable no-font fixture.
This is portable software/Core evidence, not native screen-reader, GPU or full
Alert event parity. Run CTest on Linux through
`python scripts/test_local.py --build-dir <build>`.

# API and ownership

Public headers live in `include/cui/`; generated embeddable headers in `dist/`.

```c
cui_context *ui = cui_create((cui_config){.width=800, .height=600});
cui_theme theme = cui_theme_light();
cui_begin_frame(ui, 800, 600, 1.0f/60);
cui_begin_box(ui, cui_id_from(ui, "root"), (cui_box){
    .width=-1, .height=-1, .padding=24, .gap=12,
    .background=theme.background
});
if (cui_button(ui, cui_id_from(ui, "save"), &theme,
               cui_string("Save changes"), false)) {
    /* Save application data here; explicitly invalidate if changed UI requires another frame. */
}
cui_end_box(ui);
cui_draw_list list = cui_end_frame(ui);
/* renderer.render(renderer.user, &list, theme.background); */
cui_destroy(ui);
```

Width/height zero fit contents, negative grow, positive fix logical-pixel size. Begin/end pairs must balance. Frame text and accessible names are copied into a bounded context arena. The draw list and semantic tree remain valid until the next begin; consume them synchronously or copy to host-owned storage. User strings can be transient because CUI copies them during submission. The error state is sticky until explicitly cleared; capacity errors do not authorize reuse of truncated output as complete UI.

Stable nonzero `cui_id` values are supplied by applications or derived from scoped keys. Identity follows keys when lists reorder. Duplicate public IDs and folded layout-ID collisions are errors. CUI retains focus/capture and previous regions; it does not own arbitrary domain objects or provide a general widget state registry yet. Persistent domain data and edit buffers remain app-owned.

Queue input before begin. Events are interpreted against the prior frame, then consumed once by matching controls. Multiple activations of one control in a single frame coalesce into its boolean return. The first frame has no hit regions; initialize layout before accepting interaction. Removal/disable cancels retained focus and capture. Core handles Tab/reverse Tab, Enter and release-of-Space activation. See CORE.md, EDITING.md and OVERLAYS.md for exact limits.

UI context and optional font objects require single-thread ownership. Independent contexts may be interleaved on that thread; Clay's internal current-context pointer prohibits concurrent UI calls. Host asynchronous work must hand results back on the UI thread. Optional renderers own GPU resources with their device's thread affinity; borrowed host device/window/font must outlive the renderer.

The default text measurer is approximate and unsuitable for international text.
The native text adapter supplies contextual geometry, explicit font fallback and
optional bidirectional analysis; register matching measurement and paint callbacks.
Editing offsets are UTF-8 byte indices. Explicit legacy scalar operations remain
available, while interactive editing uses grapheme/Unicode-word operations.
Consumer and platform coverage remains partial: see [editing](EDITING.md),
[contextual text](CONTEXTUAL_NATIVE_TEXT.md), [Unicode wrapping](UNICODE_WRAP.md)
and [the platform matrix](PLATFORM_MATRIX.md) for the tested contracts.

## Responsive layout and typography roles

Two header-only utilities compose existing Core behavior without global style
state or new host dependencies:

| Header | Shipped API | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cui/cui_responsive.h` | `cui_responsive_query`, `cui_responsive_at_least`, `cui_responsive_value`, `cui_responsive_fits` | [Responsive containers](RESPONSIVE_LAYOUT.md) |
| `cui/cui_typography.h` | `cui_typography_token_valid`, `cui_typography_resolve`, `cui_typography_text`, `cui_typography_text_colored` | [Reusable typography tokens](TYPOGRAPHY_TOKENS.md) |

Responsive queries use the caller's current logical container width and named
BASE/SM/MD/LG/XL/2XL thresholds. They select ordinary C box properties or whether
to submit a subtree; they do not implement CSS or own application state.
Typography roles copy caller-owned body/heading/code tokens containing supported
family/style, size, line-height, alignment and wrapping options. They do not load
fonts, synthesize faces, or add tracking/variable axes. The additional
`cui_typography_text_painted` helper supports [linear gradient text](TEXT_GRADIENT.md)
on renderers advertising the corresponding capability.
Use the same font mapping for measurement and rendering; see [Typography](TYPOGRAPHY.md).

The native dashboard launcher uses the SDL3 callback runner; consult the current
`cui_sdl3.h` and [native application guide](NATIVE_APP_STARTER.md) for host
lifecycle and live-resize constraints. Portable width policy and text roles do
not provide a native event pump themselves.

For SDL3 applications, prefer `cui_sdl3_run` for callback-driven composition during
OS-managed modal resize. Manual `cui_sdl3_poll` loops remain supported, but their
next frame can wait until the operating system releases its modal event pump.
Inside runner callbacks, `cui_sdl3_poll` synchronizes IME/cursor state without
recursively pumping events. See [Live resize](LIVE_RESIZE.md) for lifecycle,
threading, frame scheduling and scoped native validation details.

## Decoded video frames

`cui/cui_video.h` exposes a caller-owned timeline and a borrowed RGBA frame surface.
The host supplies elapsed time and already-decoded frames, handles decoder/audio
synchronization, and retains pixels until renderer consumption completes.
Generation checks reject frames retired by a seek, restart or loop.
See [the video guide](VIDEO_GUIDE.md) for ownership, commands and reproducible
headless tests. [Controlled playback controls](VIDEO_PLAYER.md) add typed host
requests and optional controls above the surface. The
[optional FFmpeg example](../examples/video_player/README.md) demonstrates silent
local-file decoding; audio, browser playback and general decoder integration
remain planned in [the video roadmap](VIDEO_PLAN.md).

# Practical application recipes

The runnable [mail fixture](../examples/native_bundle/mail.c) uses the same host
as the two-file starter. Build it from the extracted native bundle:

```sh
make APP_SOURCES="main.c mail.c" TARGET=build/mail_demo
./build/mail_demo
```

It demonstrates three independent scroll states, scoped repeated avatars/tags,
clipped long subjects, a fixed trailing star action, message selection and a
Compose/Discard preview. It has no message editor, storage, network or delivery.
It uses a desktop pane layout; narrow windows clip rather than switch navigation.
The packaging test drives real Core pointer activation for Compose/Discard,
selection and starring, then builds and captures the native executable on Xvfb.

For a mail row, cap the growing subject column as well as clipping it: an
unwrapped child's minimum width can otherwise push the timestamp/star beyond
the viewport. Keep the action column fixed. Word-wrap the reader body inside a
width-constrained scroll viewport. Give each pane its own `cui_scroll_state`.
Use `cui_scrollable_end_ex` only after a successful `cui_scrollable_begin`.
The [layout guide](LAYOUT_GUIDE.md) is the canonical sizing reference.

Use stable record keys and local IDs for repeated content; see
[IDs and lifetimes](IDS_AND_LIFETIMES.md). Use exact icon registry names from
`cui_icon.h`, check lookup results, and retain text labels for actions when an
icon is unavailable. Emoji are not a portable substitute for missing artwork.

## Sidebar custom content callbacks

`cui_sidebar_content_fn` has **four arguments**, with the user pointer last:

```c
static void folder_label(cui_context *ui, const cui_theme *theme,
                         bool collapsed, void *user) {
    const char *label = user;
    if (!collapsed)
        cui_text(ui, cui_string(label), 14, theme->sidebar_foreground);
}
```

Assign it to `label_content` and put the live label pointer in `label_user` on a
`cui_sidebar_menu_item`. Its activation callback is a different signature:
`void on_activate(void *user)`. The menu's top-level `user` feeds activation,
while `label_user`, `icon_user` and `suffix_user` feed their respective content
callbacks. Do not cast a three-argument function to the content callback type;
use the exact typedef in `include/cui/cui_sidebar.h`. Content callbacks submit
children; they do not confer generic click handling on those children.
documents.docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:
# Architecture

CUI is an experimental C11 framework with an explicit context and Clay layout adapter. `cui.h` has no SDL, OS, GPU or raw Clay API types. `cui_base.h`, editing and overlay models provide behavior; `cui_components.h` adds theme-driven painting. Platform and renderer interfaces are independent of widgets. Optional adapters are compiled integrations.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Host[Application / existing host] --> Components[Styled components + tokens]
    Host --> Base[Unstyled controls / edit / overlays]
    Components --> Base
    Base --> Core[Context / IDs / Clay / input / semantics]
    Core --> Draw[Versioned C draw list]
    Draw --> Software[Deterministic software]
    Draw --> SDL2D[SDL3 Renderer compatibility]
    Draw --> GPU[SDL_GPU / SPIR-V]
    Draw --> Sokol[Sokol / GLCORE]
    Platform[Host or SDL3 events / clipboard] --> Core
    Text[Optional FreeType + HarfBuzz] --> Core
    Text --> Software
    Text --> SDL2D
    Text --> Sokol
    Text --> GPU
```

The SDL_GPU adapter borrows an existing GPU device and claimed window. It owns its pipeline, offscreen target, glyph atlas and transfer buffer. Window input remains host responsibility. Its initial shaders are SPIR-V/Vulkan; Metal/D3D shader builds remain pending. The SDL_Renderer adapter supplies the convenience window/event loop and caches bounded glyph textures. The software renderer accepts the same command stream without a GPU.

Contexts own fixed-budget Clay memory, commands, copied frame strings, semantics and prior hit regions. UI operations are confined to one thread; switching between contexts is supported, simultaneous thread access is not. Draw-list and semantic strings expire at the next begin frame. A text editor owns bounded scratch/history while its text buffer belongs to the application. Heavy models expose explicit handles.

Events queue before begin and dispatch in order against the previous completed layout. The initial frame establishes hit regions. Core focus scopes keep modal events inside the prior top scope, route dismissal to its reducer, and restore an enabled submitted trigger. Current composition then consumes activation and builds the next semantic and paint snapshots. Native widgets and semantic adapters remain future work.

Single-TU distribution is generated from modular source; the same source compiles into a static library. Third-party source stays pinned and attributed. No JavaScript or Rust runtime is required. All 78 families remain in the status manifest; tested partial APIs are not full family verification.

The independent Sokol adapter borrows a current OpenGL context and framebuffer descriptor. It owns bounded GPU buffers, shaders and a glyph LRU; it can borrow the host Sokol runtime or initialize its own. The adapter has no SDL dependency. GLCORE is the implemented backend, with actual Intel/Mesa pixel evidence; upstream backend availability is not CUI backend support. See backends/sokol/README.md for commit ordering and ownership.

The virtual-list and dock handles retain data between frames with fixed configured capacity. Dock owns its split/tab tree and transactional restore bank; the application owns panel content. Plot scales and clipped geometry are allocation-free value operations. These are base models; their styled widgets and compound keyboard/accessibility behavior remain pending.
documents.docs/ATTACHMENT_EVENTS.md:
# Attachment action observers

Include `cui/cui_media_events.h` and call `cui_attachment_events` with the same
arguments as `cui_attachment`, plus a borrowed `cui_attachment_handler`.
It returns `control` (the legacy `cui_attachment_result`) and actual callback
counts `activation_count`, `remove_count`, `retry_count` (each zero or one).
The old options/state/result layouts and entrypoint remain unchanged.

```c
static void remove_requested(void *user, const cui_attachment_action_event *event) {
    bool *remove_after_frame = user; /* Unrelated host flag, not active card state. */
    *remove_after_frame = true;
    /* Copy *event to retain action/metadata. Do not destroy active resources here. */
}
/* During UI submission using existing caller-owned options/state/theme: */
/* cui_attachment_event_result result = cui_attachment_events(
       ui, id, theme, &state, options,
       (cui_attachment_handler){.on_remove = remove_requested, .user = &pending_remove}); */
```

Typed handlers are `on_activate` (OPEN), `on_remove` (REMOVE), `on_retry` (RETRY).
Each enables only its corresponding existing action path even if its legacy
callback is absent. Absent typed handlers retain original availability. With no
typed handlers, the facade uses the legacy operation directly. Original callbacks
always receive the untouched `options.action_user`; typed callbacks receive
`handler.user`. Other callbacks (images, children, actions, overlays) retain their
own userdata and behavior.

The complete old operation runs once. At its original callback point after paint
and tooltip work, callbacks run in fixed category order: old click, typed OPEN;
old remove, typed REMOVE; old retry, typed RETRY; then the original focus scope ends.
Absent callbacks are skipped. Repeated input coalesces into one callback per
category; media and description retry together still yield one RETRY. This is
category order, not global input order. Reading returned flags does not replay
callbacks. These are requested application actions, not proof that deletion,
opening or network retry has completed. They cannot veto an already observed
action, consume it retroactively, or become CHANGE/COMMIT/SUBMIT/lifecycle events.

Availability remains the existing planner's decision. OPEN needs an identified
card and matching handler. REMOVE also needs touch/hover and tracked card bounds.
RETRY needs identified FAILED status and matching handler. Media retry requires
media/tracked bounds; description retry is the first eligible non-title/non-custom
child. A description's individual status override does not independently gate the
retry link. Loading does **not** globally disable OPEN or REMOVE. Custom child
buttons and custom action clusters do not become these attachment actions.

ACTIVATE metadata targets the compound attachment. Genuine unique accepted
activation snapshots are copied at the actual root/button/link interaction seam,
before later custom rendering or old action callbacks can change live evidence.
`activation.target` retains the actual control ID: card, remove, media retry, or
its distinct description retry link. Multiple accepted activations/control origins
coalescing into a category produce proven-frame UNKNOWN source with no index or
activation; unavailable evidence uses the same conservative fallback. No arbitrary
first/last input is chosen. Flags establish which evidence exists.

Current Core supports LINK accessibility ACTIVATE and pointer-activatable GROUP
ACTIVATE, including the clickable card, once previous semantics register the
control. Admission before first registration fails with INVALID_ACTION. This
facade does not change routing, focus, supported actions or keyboard behavior.
Actual passive/layout-only/inert calls do not notify, while preserving legacy
work. Invalid options/pointers retain old validation behavior. No hidden heap
allocation, retained registration or input replay is added.

Payload is pointer-free and may be copied by value beyond the callback/frame.
Handler/user/payload pointer are borrowed synchronously. Legacy callbacks retain
all original side effects and must keep resources required by the remaining
operation and observers live. Typed observers must not mutate/free/rebind active
state/options/children/input/context, recursively submit UI or destroy the context.
Unrelated application flags and payload copying are allowed. Defer removal and
teardown until outer return plus renderer consumption. Resource/render callbacks
are not action observers and must retain their existing contracts.

`tests/unit/test_attachment_events.c` checks legacy/facade equivalence, availability,
userdata/order, real pointer/key/accessibility evidence, description/media retry,
ambiguity, late callback changes, custom child isolation, passive/inert scopes and
copied payload/deferred omission. The existing `media` suite covers image,
Attachment and AttachmentGroup regressions. Run native tests only through
`scripts/test_local.py`; browser/binding/full family parity is not implied.
Foreign languages retain their existing queued generic notifications; this direct
C facade does not add typed callback wrappers to them.
documents.docs/AVATAR_EVENTS.md:
# Avatar activation observation

`cui_avatar_events.h` adds an opt-in direct C observer to `cui_avatar_ex` behavior.
It does not change legacy Avatar options/layouts or the aggregate bool API.
`interactive` still enables BUTTON semantics and routing: supplying a handler to
a passive IMAGE does not turn it into a button.

```c
static void open_profile(void *user, const cui_component_event_metadata *event) {
    /* Copy *event if needed. Update application state; defer active teardown. */
    profile_owner *owner = user;
    owner->last_activation = *event;
    owner->open_requested = true;
}
/* owner remains alive through this call and the frame's render boundary. */
cui_component_action_result result = cui_avatar_events(
    ui, id, &theme, cui_string("Taylor Reed"),
    (cui_avatar_options){.interactive = true, .design_size = CUI_DESIGN_MD,
        .identity_colors = true},
    (cui_component_activation_handler){open_profile, owner});
/* Inspect counts for diagnostics; do not open the profile again from result. */
```

The complete [portable owner example](../examples/avatar_events/README.md)
contains a real owner definition and runnable model. It demonstrates a copied
payload and next-submission omission. Its synthetic accessibility input is not
native assistive-technology evidence.

The facade runs one original Avatar submission. It observes each matching event
at the existing explicit event loop after photo/icon/initial paint submission
and semantic/focus/cursor updates. Evidence is copied immediately before original
consumption; callback runs after consumption, then the loop checks the next event
live. Multiple inputs produce multiple notifications in event-index order,
including when the legacy bool would only report true once. Consuming later
input in a callback can suppress later callbacks; events are never prequeued.

`valid` reports argument preflight, not successful rendering. `submitted` reports
ordinary active paint-enabled, non-inert submission, including disabled and
passive avatars. `activation_count` counts observed legacy activation-loop
matches when submitted; a missing handler still counts and consumes as before.
`request_count` is always zero. Counts saturate at `SIZE_MAX`, setting
`count_overflow`; callback delivery continues. Copying/reading results does not
redispatch. Omission, disabled/passive/inert/layout-only work does not invent a
notification. The legacy API's own return/consume behavior remains unchanged.

Metadata kind is ACTIVATE and target is the Avatar ID. Genuine accepted snapshots
preserve frame, event index, input source and contact/key evidence. When the old
activation gate matches but Core cannot establish accepted evidence, notification
has proven frame only with UNKNOWN source and no index/activation flags. A
regression reproduces this honestly using a genuine pointer event plus a
sticky duplicate-semantic Core error. It does not fabricate a snapshot or claim
that preflight validity clears a Core error.

Avatar preserves default Core keyboard behavior: Enter nonrepeat key-down and
Space release after capture. It does not adopt source Button's different release
policy. Accessibility ACTIVATE needs prior supported semantics; failed admission
before registration is not an activation. Core evidence is separate from tested
native screen-reader integration.

Handler/user/payload pointers are borrowed synchronously; metadata is pointer-free
and copyable beyond frame/context lifetime. Existing pixels, caches, labels,
icons and users retain their rendering lifetimes. Updating unrelated application
flags and consuming later input are supported. Do not rebind/free active
resources, recursively submit the same component/frame or destroy context in a
callback. Request omission/teardown in application state, then apply it after
outer return and renderer consumption. No runtime destruction guard, owner veto,
CHANGE/COMMIT/SUBMIT, image loading lifecycle or foreign-language callback facade
is introduced.

## Stack activations

`cui_avatar_stack_events` adds the separately reviewed stack observer while
`cui_avatar_stack` retains its old aggregate index API:

```c
static void choose_person(void *user, const cui_avatar_stack_activation *event) {
    team_owner *owner = user;
    owner->chosen_index = event->index;
    owner->chosen_key = event->key;
    owner->last_activation = event->event;
}
cui_avatar_stack_event_result result = cui_avatar_stack_events(
    ui, id, &theme, people, people_count,
    (cui_avatar_stack_options){.size = 48, .interactive = true},
    (cui_avatar_stack_handler){choose_person, owner});
```

Callbacks follow visible child submission order, then that child's event-index
order. They are not sorted across the compound by input chronology. For events
on children 2, 0 and 1 in that time order, callbacks report children 0, 1 and 2;
`result.control` is 2, preserving the highest activated visible index returned
by the old API. Several events on one child generate several callbacks.
`result.action` uses the same validity/submission/count/overflow fields as the
single Avatar; request_count stays zero. A missing handler still counts and
preserves the legacy aggregate index and consumption.

The payload's metadata target is the stack ID, while genuine activation evidence
retains its child target. Index and application key are copied from the actual
visible iteration, including an original zero key. Nonzero keys retain stable
child identity across reorder; zero retains the existing index-based identity
rule. The payload does not replace zero with a generated key. A frame-only
fallback has no claimed child activation snapshot; index/key still identify the
actual legacy iteration. The regression exercises this with real routed input
and a duplicate-semantic Core error.

Width-limited hidden items and passive overflow never notify. Existing overlap
hit order, default visible count, images, semantics and appearance remain
unchanged. Active item arrays are borrowed and must not be mutated/rebound/freed
inside callbacks. Consuming later input can suppress later events/children; no
queue or replay is introduced. Resource lifetimes and deferred teardown rules
are identical to the single-Avatar observer.

The [checkpoint](design/AVATAR_EVENTS_SLICE.md) remains the reviewed design
history. Complete Avatar parity is not claimed. Integrator work includes test/
module registration, generated SDK/API/skill exports and honest binding
availability; a C declaration copied into an SDK does not expose a working
foreign callback facade.
documents.docs/AVATAR_FAILURE_AUDIT.md:
# Avatar failure and naming audit

Reference: GPUI Kit 0.7.1, commit
`87d10ae5e1299d1be18670a37570c5402f952e34`, inspected from the local
reference checkout recorded in `docs/upstream-baseline.md`.

`crates/base/src/avatar.rs`, `Avatar::render`, chooses its optional image slot
before its fallback slot. `AvatarImage::render` delegates to `gpui::Img`.
There is no Avatar load-state callback, error transition or retry mechanism.
The base tests assert image-slot precedence and fallback when the slot is absent;
they do not assert fallback after decoding failure.

`crates/component/src/avatar/avatar.rs`, `Avatar::render`, always constructs a
fallback and adds an image slot when `src` exists. Without `src`, a supplied name
selects initials and identity colors; without a name it selects the configurable
placeholder icon. This does not establish automatic failed-image fallback or
accessible-name behavior. GPUI image internals are outside this bounded audit.

CUI accepts host-decoded RGBA, validates it synchronously and paints initials
when the current source/cache cannot prepare. Preparation failure leaves a prior
cache intact; `cui_avatar_ex` gates rendering on the current return value rather
than the cache's `ready` flag. A valid source on a later frame recovers. No
production behavior change or speculative lifecycle API is needed.

`tests/unit/test_content.c`, `image_avatars`, exercises successful rendering,
missing and invalid-stride sources after success, preserved cache, initials draw
commands, software fallback pixels, full-name image/button and anonymous image semantics, and recovery of
the photo without unnecessary cache revision changes. Fallback text commands are asserted independently of the software fill checks,
which omit text to avoid a host-font dependency. CUI uses Anonymous for unnamed
extended avatars. Semantic names are checked before the next frame starts.

This slice does not establish complete Avatar parity. Configurable upstream icon
placeholders, identity colors and typography/size variants remain outside this
failure-and-naming evidence. There is no host image acquisition, decoder, network
retry, screen-reader integration or GPU coverage in these tests.
documents.docs/AVATAR_MESSAGE_EXAMPLES.md:
# Profile images and compact conversations

Avatar now accepts a borrowed RGBA bitmap through `cui_avatar_ex`. The legacy
`cui_avatar` initials API is unchanged. The gallery uses three original fictional
portraits, processed by the pinned `scripts/generate_avatar_assets.py` script.
The same masked pixels enter the native and WASM draw lists; no DOM image is used.

Initialize a caller-owned cache once, outside the frame loop. Retain the source
pixels, cache object and destination storage until rendering has completed.
Changing the source pointer, dimensions, stride or revision rebuilds the cache.
Increment the source revision when its pixels change. There is no per-frame heap
allocation and no cleanup function: the application owns all storage. A diameter
of 1–512 is supported; storage requires diameter × diameter × 4 bytes. Source and
cache storage must not overlap. Missing or invalid images fall back to initials. A
failed preparation leaves the last successful cache intact, but `cui_avatar_ex`
uses the current preparation result and never displays that stale photo for an
invalid source. To represent acquisition/decode failure or a pending download,
pass a zero bitmap; retry with valid borrowed RGBA pixels when available. Recovery
can reuse the same cache. Acquisition, decoding and retry policy belong to the
host; there is no network or asynchronous source-status API.

The supplied full name labels both photo and initials frames; it is not shortened
for assistive technology. An empty name becomes “Anonymous” in `cui_avatar_ex`.
Passive avatars expose image semantics and interactive avatars expose button
semantics. Read semantic records within the current frame lifetime; copy names
before retaining them across frames. These names are a CUI accessibility policy:
the frozen upstream Avatar does not define an equivalent automatic name policy.
See `docs/AVATAR_FAILURE_AUDIT.md` for the precise frozen upstream distinction.

```c
#include <cui/cui_content.h>
static unsigned char circle_pixels[96 * 96 * 4];
static cui_avatar_image circle;

bool profile_init(void) {
    return cui_avatar_image_init(&circle, circle_pixels, sizeof circle_pixels, 96);
}

bool profile_draw(cui_context *ui, const cui_theme *theme, cui_bitmap borrowed) {
    return cui_avatar_ex(ui, cui_id_from(ui, "profile"), theme, cui_string("Alex Morgan"),
        (cui_avatar_options){.size = 48, .ring_width = 2,
            .image = borrowed, .image_state = &circle, .interactive = true});
}
```

Opt into named initials colors with `.identity_colors = true`. The palette uses
`theme.dark` and the frozen twelve 30-degree OkLCH hues. The default assignment
hashes the UTF-8 bytes of CUI's initials using 32-bit FNV-1a; this is stable within
CUI but differs from GPUI's private hash and initials rules. Set
`.custom_identity_hue = true, .identity_hue = 0` to choose a hue index in 0–11.
Invalid overrides retain legacy colors. Explicit `custom_background` and
`custom_foreground` override the palette; initials keep the identity outline.
Photos and anonymous placeholders keep neutral outlines. `cui_avatar_identity`
exposes the same palette for application composition and leaves output untouched
on invalid arguments.

`.anonymous_icon = true` replaces the empty-name question mark with the default
User SVG. `.placeholder_name = cui_string("building-2")` selects a named icon;
a borrowed `.placeholder` points to an existing `cui_icon_state` for custom SVG.
The typed state wins over a name. A supplied name still selects initials, and a
valid photo still wins over both. All icons remain decorative within the existing
Avatar image/button semantic record; the anonymous accessible name stays
“Anonymous”. SVG loading errors follow the existing Icon contract and do not
silently substitute a different glyph. Keep borrowed icon state and mask versions
alive until rendering finishes; collect or destroy only afterward. Named icons
use the bounded context cache, whose draw borrows expire at the next frame.

`.design_size` opts into the shared `CUI_DESIGN_XS` through `CUI_DESIGN_9XL` scale.
An explicit variant wins over `.size`; `INHERIT` keeps the existing custom diameter
and .38 text ratio. `.rem_size = 0` uses 16 logical pixels per rem; positive values
up to 512 scale variant geometry and typography. No fonts are loaded implicitly.
Use `cui_avatar_measure` to inspect the resulting diameter, text size and weight.

| Variant | Diameter at rem=16 | Initials text | Weight |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| XS | 16 | 10.4 | normal |
| SM | 24 | 12 | normal |
| BASE / MD | 48 | 14 | normal |
| LG | 80 | 30 | semibold |
| XL through 9XL | 2 × shared control height, capped at 512 | shared font size × 30/18 | semibold |

The first four sizes reproduce frozen Avatar preset geometry and text sizes.
BASE aliases MD. XL through 9XL extend CUI's shared design scale; they are not
upstream presets. Their diameters are 96, 112, 128, 160, 208, 256, 304, 400 and
512 at rem=16. The overall scale is capped when the raw diameter would exceed 512, reducing
both diameter and font size together to preserve their ratio. This also applies
to 9XL at rem=16, whose raw diameter is 528.
Custom GPUI `Size` sets initials-child dimensions; CUI does not claim identical
custom text layout. Invalid variants or rem values fall back to legacy metrics.
These opt-ins do not change `cui_avatar` or `cui_avatar_stack` defaults.

`cui_avatar_stack` takes up to 64 items with stable application keys. Its default
shows three portraits and a passive overflow count. Later portraits paint and
receive pointer hits above earlier portraits. Positive `width` reduces the number
shown to fit; zero uses the intrinsic width. Interactive stacks return the selected
item index, or `SIZE_MAX`. Disabled items retain their semantics and reject
activation. Cursor and interaction state use the shared Core hooks. The image name
is its accessible name; interactive portraits use button semantics.

Message separates avatar, header, body and footer callbacks. Put sender and time
in the header, one message in the body, and delivery/reaction controls in the
footer. The gallery demonstrates incoming and outgoing rows, portrait callbacks,
controlled acknowledgement and an actual reaction callback. `max_bubble_width`
caps the content column while preserving the available row width and START/END
alignment. Zero preserves the existing layout. The footer inset uses the actual
avatar width and row gap. MessageScroller uses the same row composition with
stable IDs and a virtualized conversation model. Slots are inferred present from
`present`, nonempty text or a render callback; omit a slot by clearing all three.
Scroll deltas that change MessageScroller position are consumed, allowing an
ongoing touch pan to remain internal; refused boundary deltas can reach the host.

```c
#include <cui/cui_message.h>
void conversation_row(cui_context *ui, cui_id id, const cui_theme *theme,
                      cui_message_options slots) {
    cui_message_body body = {
        .slot = {.text = cui_string("Can you review the release notes?")},
        .typed_bubble = true, .bubble = CUI_BUBBLE_SECONDARY};
    slots.header.text = cui_string("Alex Morgan · 09:30");
    slots.body = &body;
    slots.body_count = 1;
    slots.footer.text = cui_string("Delivered · 09:30");
    slots.width = 600;
    slots.max_bubble_width = 280;
    slots.alignment = CUI_MESSAGE_START;
    slots.name = cui_string("Message from Alex");
    cui_message(ui, id, theme, slots);
}
```

The reusable API accepts pixels supplied by the application; it does not decode
PNG files or manage image downloads. Applications own conversation/session state
and callback lifetimes. These examples do not implement a network messaging
service, attachments or a complete messaging accessibility model.

Validation includes headless cover-crop/alpha/cache/revision checks, native
software rendering, overlap hit order, keyboard activation, disabled and cancelled
touch activation, and actual compact message bounds in both alignments. The
Chromium suite uses CDP touch contacts for profile selection, reactions and virtual
scrolling, checks actual WASM portrait pixels and circular alpha, all seven bubble
variants and 390px layouts. This is Chromium evidence, not physical iOS/Android
or full platform parity.

# Avatar style bindings

The retained bridge exposes opt-in Avatar styling in C, Python, Node/TypeScript,
Go and Rust. Shared `design_size` currently covers **Button and Avatar only**;
other component kinds return an error. This is an incremental binding surface,
not uniform styling coverage or full component parity.

The existing Button `size` method, convenience variants, defaults and callback
behavior remain unchanged. `design_size` on Button selects the same scale;
subsequent size calls replace the previous selection. The C
`cui_bridge_design_size` typedef aliases `cui_bridge_button_size`, retaining all
existing `CUI_BRIDGE_SIZE_*` values. Go `DesignSize` and Rust `DesignSize` likewise
alias their existing `Size` type; Python and TypeScript expose named size literals.

| Setter | Coverage | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `design_size(size)` | Button, Avatar | `inherit`, `xs`, `sm`, `base`, `md`, `lg`, `xl`, `2xl` through `9xl` |
| `identity_colors(enabled, hue)` | Avatar | Deterministic CUI identity palette; optional hue selects one of 12 hues, 0..11 |
| `anonymous_icon(enabled, name)` | Avatar | Named SVG fallback for an empty person name; empty icon name selects `user` |

C uses `cui_bridge_set_design_size`, `cui_bridge_set_avatar_identity` and
`cui_bridge_set_avatar_placeholder`. Boolean flags must be 0/1; hue must be
0..11. Placeholder names are validated UTF-8 and copied transactionally, with a
4096-byte limit. Invalid calls preserve the previous settings. Removed handles
and closed Apps return the existing handle/lifecycle errors. An App pointer is
invalid after `cui_bridge_destroy`, as with every bridge function.

Python, Node and Go support configuring an unmounted retained builder and live
updates after mounting. Rust supports the App methods and fluent borrowed
Builder methods. All wrappers validate component kinds and argument types;
invalid Go builder calls retain the existing sticky error convention.

```python
person = avatar("person", "Ada Lovelace").design_size("md").identity_colors(True, 4)
anonymous = avatar("anonymous").anonymous_icon(True, "user")
```

```typescript
const person = avatar('person', 'Ada Lovelace').design_size('md').identity_colors(true, 4);
const anonymous = avatar('anonymous').anonymous_icon(true, 'user');
```

```go
person := cui.Avatar("person", "Ada Lovelace").DesignSize(cui.MD).IdentityColors(true, 4)
anonymous := cui.Avatar("anonymous", "").AnonymousIcon(true, "user")
// IdentityColors(true) selects the deterministic hue; at most one hue is accepted.
```

```rust
let person = app.build_child(root, Kind::Avatar, "person")?
    .text("Ada Lovelace")?.design_size(DesignSize::Md)?
    .identity_colors(true, Some(4))?.finish();
app.anonymous_icon(person, true, "user")?;
// None selects the deterministic hue.
```

With every new option disabled and size inherited, Avatar retains its exact
legacy renderer: 40 logical pixels by default, or its existing `visual_size`
width. Explicit scale variants take precedence over pixel width and use the
native Avatar's 16px rem basis: XS=16, SM=24, BASE=MD=48, LG=80; larger variants
follow the shared scale with a 512px bound. Styled inherited pixel sizes are
also capped to 512. Clearing the scale, identity and anonymous-icon options
restores the legacy renderer, including legacy pixel widths over 512. Positive
Avatar dimensions stay fixed even in narrow flex layouts; this slice adds no
responsive shrink behavior. Avatar continues to ignore `visual_size` height.

Identity colors use the native CUI initials hash and current theme's light/dark
palette. They are not a guarantee of another toolkit's identity assignment.
Named people keep their initials even when an anonymous icon is enabled.
The anonymous icon is decorative within the Avatar's existing Image semantic;
it does not add a focus stop or activation/callback API. Icon names resolve via
the existing embedded catalog/name/path aliases and context cache, with runtime
SVG rasterization. An unavailable icon name paints no icon; it is not a raw SVG
string, arbitrary filesystem loader or a foreign icon-state object.

This slice omits borrowed `cui_icon_state *`, raw SVG input/custom loaders,
bitmap/image-state ownership, custom background/foreground/ring colors,
interactivity and AvatarStack. It does not add style setters to other components.
Use a matching bridge/library revision; generated SDK/export copies are updated
by the integration workflow.

Validation includes a portable real-bridge draw fixture covering legacy and
styled bounds, palette colors, SVG mask draw commands, accessible Image/name,
owned placeholder lifetime, transactional rejection, removal and closed Apps.
The fixture includes the portable bridge implementation to inspect its private
renderer without exporting a testing hook; compile it with the `cui` target
only, not `cui_bridge`. Existing callback/lifetime tests and new language cases
cover all five handwritten surfaces, including strict TypeScript negative checks.
All CTest runs use `python scripts/test_local.py --build-dir <build>` on Linux.

# Avatar palette, placeholder and metrics audit

Frozen reference: GPUI Kit 0.7.1 commit
`87d10ae5e1299d1be18670a37570c5402f952e34`.

Sources: `crates/component/src/avatar/avatar.rs`, `avatar/mod.rs`,
`website/component/avatar.md` and `website/base/primitives/avatar.md`.
The base guide describes parent-supplied loading/error fallback content; it does
not establish an automatic Avatar error transition.

The styled Avatar chooses an image when supplied, initials when a name exists,
and a configurable `Icon` placeholder otherwise. Its default icon is User.
Initials carry a 12-hue identity palette; photo/anonymous borders remain neutral.
Each palette hue is 30 degrees apart in OkLCH. Light palette triples
(background, foreground, border) are (0.97,0.032), (0.50,0.145), (0.89,0.05);
dark triples are (0.30,0.05), (0.82,0.11), (0.36,0.06). The hue index is selected
by private GPUI hashing of the short name. CUI must disclose a different stable
hash assignment if it does not port that implementation.

Frozen metrics are XS=16px with 0.65rem text; Small=24px with 0.75rem text;
Medium=48px with 0.875rem text; Large=80px with 1.875rem semibold text.
Custom `Size` sets the initials child dimensions to half the avatar dimensions;
it does not clearly specify half-size text. Do not claim such typography parity.
Additional CUI design-scale sizes must be identified as extensions.

Remaining broader differences include upstream Unicode uppercasing/initial
selection versus CUI first/last UTF-8 scalar initials, arbitrary GPUI style
refinements, and arbitrary base fallback children. This audit does not establish
complete Avatar or AvatarGroup parity.

Implemented opt-in mapping: `cui_avatar_options.design_size` reuses the shared
CUI scale. INHERIT retains existing `.size` behavior. Explicit XS/SM/BASE=MD/LG
use the frozen preset dimensions above. XL..9XL use twice shared control height,
with the overall scale capped at 512 divided by raw variant diameter; typography
uses shared font size times 30/18,
with semibold weight. The cap scales diameter and text together to preserve
their ratio, including 9XL at rem=16. These higher steps are CUI extensions. A positive rem
parameter scales presets; zero in options selects 16. Metrics helper rejects
invalid inputs without modifying output, while Avatar falls back to legacy
metrics for invalid options.

Identity colors use the frozen OkLCH triples and theme.dark. CUI deliberately
uses FNV-1a over its UTF-8 initials bytes, not an unverifiable GPUI hash clone.
An explicit 0..11 override supports host-controlled assignment. Explicit legacy
background/foreground options still win. Invalid hue overrides retain legacy
colors. The identity border applies only to named initials frames.

Anonymous SVG rendering is opt-in, with borrowed typed state, then named
context-cache lookup, then User as the default. The Icon contract determines
lookup/parse failures. A photo or supplied name wins; decorative SVGs add no
semantic duplication. Typed-mask lifetime and named-cache bounds stay those of
the existing Icon API. No network source acquisition is added.

Headless tests in `tests/unit/test_content.c`, `avatar_variants`, check all
light/dark palette hues for AA contrast after 8-bit encoding and non-clipped
border channels, hash stability across identical initials, rejected hue overrides,
all design sizes, explicit metrics precedence, rem scaling, typography weights,
legacy metrics/colors, typed/named/default icons, initials precedence, image
precedence, absence of duplicate semantics, and software pixels. The targeted
content CTest uses the isolated-display wrapper; no GPU or screen-reader claim
is implied. Generated SDK/skill metadata remains an integrator refresh step.

The scale-cap regression exercises every variant at rem 1, 16, 64 and 512,
checks the font-size/diameter ratio against uncapped small-rem metrics, and
verifies actual Avatar bounds and emitted text sizes. Large rem values cannot
leave oversized initials after the diameter reaches 512.

# Portable backgrounds and bitmap effects

`cui_effects.h` generates reusable RGBA8 pixels in caller-owned storage. It uses
only core CUI types and portable C11, with no allocation or platform dependency.
All functions return false for invalid input before writing output. Row padding
is preserved. The caller must provide actual storage matching the declared sizes;
source `cui_bitmap` follows the core borrowed-storage contract.

`cui_effect_linear_gradient` accepts ordered color stops and a finite angle in
degrees. Zero runs left to right, 90 top to bottom, 180 right to left. Angles span
the projected pixel-center bounds, so the first and last projected corners sample
0 and 1 exactly. One-pixel images sample 0. Stops must increase strictly within
[0,1]; colors outside the stop interval extend to the edges. Interpolation uses
premultiplied sRGB values, then writes straight-alpha RGBA8. This avoids hidden
transparent colors leaking into visible gradient pixels; it is not linear-light
or Oklab interpolation.

`cui_effect_opacity` scales alpha without scaling RGB, which is correct for the
straight-alpha pixels required by `cui_bitmap`. Use `cui_bitmap_paint.opacity` for
draw-time fading when regenerated pixels are unnecessary. Existing `cui_box`
opacity also applies to descendants. Color fills use `cui_box.background`.

`cui_effect_blur` is a separable box blur with replicated edge samples. Its radius
is a pixel radius, not a CSS Gaussian blur length. It processes premultiplied RGBA
in caller-owned float scratch, then returns straight-alpha pixels; fully
transparent results have RGB zero. Query scratch with
`cui_effect_blur_scratch_floats`, allocate that many floats once, and reuse them.
Zero from this query indicates invalid dimensions or size overflow. Scratch must
be float-aligned, large enough, and disjoint from both images. Source/destination
may use identical pointers and strides, or disjoint storage; partial overlap is
rejected. Radius zero copies the original bytes, including transparent RGB.
The sliding-window implementation runs in O(width * height), including for very
large radii. This is a single box pass, not a Gaussian approximation.

Paint generated pixels through `cui_paint_bitmap` with an explicit opacity of 1
and a box radius for rounded corners. Alternatively use the existing bitmap
underlay API to place them behind content. Keep the pixels alive through renderer
completion; increment bitmap revision whenever pixels change so adapters can
refresh cached uploads. Reuse generated backgrounds instead of recalculating
unchanged gradients or blurs every frame.

A backdrop blur requires the host to capture the pixels behind the element and
supply that bitmap to `cui_effect_blur`. These primitives do not capture a native
window, sample earlier draw commands, or provide automatic CSS backdrop-filter
behavior. They can blur an image, a generated background, or a host-supplied
capture. Host capture coordinates, timing, and upload remain host responsibilities.

`examples/effects/background.c` provides a reusable slate-to-teal gradient tile
and a rounded painting helper. Initialize its caller-owned state once, then paint
it inside a CUI frame. This example has no host or renderer dependency.
